## Part I — From Insurance to Data Science

### Why Data Science in Insurance?

Insurance is fundamentally concerned with making decisions under uncertainty.

As actuaries, we use probability, statistics, and insurance principles to assess risk. In practice, these decisions also require reliable data and systematic methods for analysing it.

For example, a motor insurer may want to determine whether claim frequency differs according to:

- age;
- geographical area;
- vehicle characteristics; or
- other characteristics of policyholders.

Data science provides a framework for investigating such questions.

### Data-Driven Insurance Decisions

An insurance decision is **data-driven** when relevant data are used systematically to support the decision.

Data do not replace actuarial judgement. They provide evidence that can be combined with:

- statistical methods;
- insurance knowledge; and
- professional judgement.

Insurers use data to:

- assess and classify risks during underwriting;
- estimate claim frequency and claim severity;
- determine appropriate premiums;
- monitor claims and identify unusual patterns;
- evaluate portfolio experience; and
- support risk-management decisions.

### From Data to Decision

Consider a motor insurance portfolio.

Suppose an insurer observes that policyholders in different age groups have different claim frequencies.

The insurer needs to determine whether this difference is supported by sufficient data and whether age should be considered when assessing risk.

$$
\text{Insurance problem}
\rightarrow
\text{Data}
\rightarrow
\text{Analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision}.
$$

The purpose of data science is therefore to transform data into useful information and evidence for decision-making.

### Data Do Not Speak for Themselves

Observed patterns in insurance data must be interpreted in context.

A difference between two groups does not necessarily imply that the corresponding risk factor causes the difference.

When interpreting an observed pattern, we should consider:

- data quality;
- exposure;
- other relevant risk factors; and
- the method of analysis.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

**An observed pattern is evidence, not automatically an explanation.**

Data science helps us identify and quantify patterns, while actuarial judgement is needed to interpret those patterns in context.

:::

### From Risk to Data

The concepts of risk introduced in Chapter 1 are theoretical.

In practice, quantities such as probabilities and expected losses must be estimated from observations.

Suppose an insurer wants to estimate claim frequency from historical data.

A simple estimate is

$$
\widehat{\lambda}
=
\frac{\text{Number of claims}}
{\text{Exposure}}.
$$

The estimate is obtained from observed insurance experience.

### Estimating Claim Severity

Suppose the observed claim amounts are

$$
X_1,\ldots,X_n.
$$

A basic estimate of the average claim amount is

$$
\widehat{\mu}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
$$

More advanced statistical methods can then be used to investigate how claim severity varies with different risk characteristics.

### From Risk to Risk Assessment

The transition from actuarial theory to data analysis can be summarised as

$$
\boxed{
\text{Risk}
\rightarrow
\text{Observable outcomes}
\rightarrow
\text{Data}
\rightarrow
\text{Statistical analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{Risk assessment}
}
$$

Data science provides a systematic framework for the stages involving:

- data collection;
- data preparation;
- exploration;
- analysis and modelling; and
- communication.

### Exposure Matters

Insurance experience cannot always be compared using raw claim counts.

A portfolio with more policies or a longer observation period will generally produce more claims simply because there is more opportunity for claims to occur.

Therefore, insurance experience is often measured relative to an appropriate measure of **exposure**.

For example,

$$
\text{Claim frequency}
=
\frac{\text{Number of claims}}
{\text{Exposure}}.
$$

::: {.callout-important}

## Key idea

**Raw claim counts are not sufficient for comparing insurance risk.**

The amount of exposure must be considered when measuring claim experience.

:::

### Why Data Science Matters to Actuaries

Modern insurance problems often involve large and complex datasets.

An actuary may need to:

- combine information from different sources;
- identify data-quality problems;
- explore relationships between variables;
- develop statistical models; and
- communicate analytical results.

However, applying an algorithm to a dataset is not sufficient.

Actuarial knowledge is needed to formulate the problem, select meaningful variables, recognise appropriate exposure measures, assess assumptions, and interpret the results.

### Data Science and Actuarial Science

| Data science | Actuarial science |
|---|---|
| Collects and prepares data | Understands the insurance problem |
| Explores and visualises data | Interprets risk and uncertainty |
| Develops statistical and predictive models | Assesses actuarial assumptions and implications |
| Communicates analytical results | Applies professional judgement to decisions |

The two disciplines are complementary.

$$
\boxed{
\text{Data}
+
\text{Statistical methods}
+
\text{Computing}
+
\text{Actuarial judgement}
}
$$

provides a framework for making better-informed insurance decisions.

## Part II — What Is Data Science?

### What Is Data Science?

Data science is concerned with extracting useful information and knowledge from data to support:

- understanding;
- prediction; and
- decision-making.

It combines:

- statistical methods;
- computational tools; and
- knowledge of the subject area in which the data arise.

There is no single method that defines data science.

Different problems require different combinations of data management, statistical analysis, programming, visualisation, and modelling.

### Data Science in Insurance

For an insurer, data science can be used to investigate questions such as:

- How does claim frequency vary across different groups of policyholders?
- Which characteristics are associated with larger claims?
- Can future claims be predicted from available information?
- Are there unusual patterns in claims that require further investigation?

These questions require more than calculating statistics.

They require:

- an understanding of the insurance problem;
- appropriate data;
- suitable analytical methods; and
- computational tools.

### Four Foundations of Data Science

Data science brings together four closely related components:

1. **Data**
2. **Statistics**
3. **Computing**
4. **Domain knowledge**

Each component contributes something different to the analysis.

### The Four Foundations

![The Four Foundations of Data Science](figures/Four_Foundations_of_Data_Science.png){#fig-foundations-slides fig-align="center" width=85%}

### Data

**Data** provide the observations from which information can be obtained.

In insurance, data may include:

- policy characteristics;
- exposure;
- claims;
- claim amounts;
- premiums; and
- other information relevant to risk.

Without appropriate data, statistical analysis cannot provide useful evidence about the insurance problem.

### Statistics

**Statistics** provides methods for:

- describing data;
- identifying patterns;
- quantifying uncertainty; and
- drawing conclusions from observations.

For example, an insurer may use statistical methods to estimate claim frequency or compare the experience of different groups.

### Computing

**Computing** provides tools for:

- storing data;
- manipulating data;
- analysing data; and
- visualising data.

Modern datasets may contain thousands or millions of observations.

Computational tools make it possible to carry out analyses efficiently and reproducibly.

### Domain Knowledge

**Domain knowledge** provides an understanding of the context in which the data arise.

For an actuary, this includes knowledge of:

- insurance products;
- risk;
- exposure;
- claims;
- premiums; and
- the business decisions that the analysis is intended to support.

### The Four Components Are Complementary

The four components work together.

Suppose an insurer observes that one group of policyholders has a higher claim frequency than another.

- **Statistics** can quantify the difference.
- **Computing** can process the underlying data.
- **Domain knowledge** can determine whether the comparison is meaningful.
- **Data** provide the observations on which the analysis is based.

The analysis may also need to account for exposure and other characteristics that differ between the groups.

### Data Science Is More Than Programming

Programming is an important tool in data science.

However, data science is not simply programming with data.

A successful analysis requires:

- an appropriate question;
- reliable data;
- suitable statistical methods; and
- an understanding of the context in which the results will be used.

| Component | Main purpose | Example in insurance |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Provide observations | Policy and claims records |
| Statistics | Quantify and analyse patterns | Estimate claim frequency |
| Computing | Process and analyse data efficiently | Use R to manipulate and model data |
| Domain knowledge | Interpret results in context | Understand exposure and insurance risk |

### Data Science and Decision-Making

The ultimate purpose of data science is not to produce tables, graphs, or models for their own sake.

Its purpose is to provide evidence that can improve decisions.

A useful framework is

$$
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Data}
\rightarrow
\text{Analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision}.
$$

For example, an insurer may investigate whether a particular characteristic should be used in pricing.

The analysis may involve historical policy and claims data, data preparation, exploration, and statistical modelling.

The resulting evidence can then be considered as part of the pricing decision.

### From Analysis to Action

A useful data-science result should answer three questions:

1. **What did the data show?**
2. **How reliable is the evidence?**
3. **What decision, if any, should follow from it?**

The quality of a decision depends on more than the predictive performance of a model.

We must also consider:

- the quality and relevance of the data; assumptions underlying the analysis;
- uncertainty in the results; and the consequences of using the results.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

**Data science provides analytical evidence; actuarial judgement provides the insurance context needed to interpret and use that evidence.**

:::


## Part III — The Role of Data in Insurance

### The Role of Data in Insurance

Data provide the empirical foundation for many insurance activities.

Insurers collect and maintain information about:

- policies and policyholders;
- exposure;
- premiums;
- claims; and
- payments.

These data support decisions about:

- underwriting;
- pricing;
- claims management; and
- risk management.

### What Makes Insurance Data Useful?

The usefulness of insurance data depends on more than the amount of information available.

Data should be:

- relevant to the problem;
- recorded consistently;
- sufficiently complete; and
- sufficiently accurate for the intended analysis.

Insurance data must also be interpreted in relation to **exposure** and the characteristics of the insurance portfolio.

### Why Claim Counts Are Not Enough

Suppose two portfolios have:

- Portfolio A: 1,000 claims;
- Portfolio B: 500 claims.

We cannot conclude that Portfolio A has twice the claim risk.

Portfolio A may simply have substantially more exposure.

A more meaningful comparison is often based on **claim frequency**:

$$
\text{Claim frequency}
=
\frac{\text{Number of claims}}
{\text{Exposure}}.
$$

::: {.callout-important}

## Key idea

**Insurance experience should be interpreted relative to the amount of exposure.**

Raw counts alone may give a misleading comparison between portfolios.

:::

### Insurance Data Sources

Insurance data come from both **internal** and **external** sources.

Common internal sources include:

- **Policy data** — policy type, coverage, dates, insured characteristics, and premium.
- **Exposure data** — the amount of time or risk exposure associated with a policy.
- **Claims data** — claim dates, types, status, and amounts.
- **Payment data** — premiums, claim payments, expenses, and other transactions.
- **Customer data** — policyholder characteristics and interactions with the insurer.

### External Data

External sources may provide information relevant to risk assessment.

Examples include:

- geographical information;
- demographic information;
- weather data;
- economic indicators; and
- other publicly or commercially available data.

These data may provide information that is not available from the insurer's own records.

### Combining Data Sources

Insurance information is often stored in different systems.

For example:

$$
\text{Policy system}
\qquad
\text{Claims system}
\qquad
\text{Payment system}
$$

may contain different parts of the information required for an analysis.

These sources may need to be linked using a common identifier, such as a policy number or claim number.

$$
\text{Policy data}
+
\text{Exposure data}
+
\text{Claims data}
\longrightarrow
\text{Insurance analysis}.
$$

### Start with the Question

The objective of data collection is **not** to collect as much data as possible.

The data should be:

- relevant to the question;
- measured appropriately; and
- suitable for the intended analysis.

The question should determine which data are required.

::: {.callout-note}

## Start with the question

**Do not begin with "What data do we have?"**

Begin with:

> **What question are we trying to answer?**

Then determine what data are needed to answer it.

:::

### Types of Data

Insurance datasets contain variables with different characteristics.

Recognising the type of each variable is important because it affects how the variable can be:

- summarised;
- visualised; and
- analysed.

A useful first distinction is between:

$$
\boxed{\text{Categorical data}}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{\text{Numerical data}}.
$$

### Categorical Data

**Categorical data** describe membership in a group or category.

Examples in insurance include:

- type of insurance;
- geographical area;
- vehicle type;
- policy status; and
- claim type.

For example:

```text
Area = Urban
Area = Rural
```

The values identify categories rather than numerical quantities.

### Numerical Data

**Numerical data** represent quantities for which arithmetic operations are meaningful.

Examples include:

* age;
* exposure;
* premium;
* number of claims; and
* claim amount.

Numerical variables can be further classified as **discrete** or **continuous**.

### Discrete and Continuous Data

A **discrete variable** takes values that can be counted.

For example, the number of claims satisfies

$$
N \in {0,1,2,\ldots}.
$$

A **continuous variable** can take values within an interval.

Examples include:

* claim amount; and
* exposure,

depending on how the quantities are measured and recorded.

### Structured and Unstructured Data

Another useful distinction is between **structured** and **unstructured** data.

**Structured data** are organised in a predefined format, such as rows and columns in a database.

Examples:

* policy records;
* claims records; and
* customer databases.

**Unstructured data** do not follow a predefined tabular structure.

Examples include:

* documents;
* images;
* audio; and
* text.

For introductory actuarial analysis, structured data are particularly important.

### Types of Insurance Variables

| Variable         | Example | Type                  |
| ---------------- | ------: | --------------------- |
| Age              |      35 | Numerical             |
| Area             |   Urban | Categorical           |
| Exposure         |    0.75 | Numerical, continuous |
| Number of claims |       2 | Numerical, discrete   |
| Claim amount     |  18,500 | Numerical             |
| Policy status    |  Active | Categorical           |

The classification affects the methods that can be used.

For example:

* numerical distributions can be examined using histograms;
* categorical frequencies can be displayed using bar charts.

### Variable Type and Variable Role

The **type** of a variable and its **role** in an analysis are different concepts.

For example, `Claim Amount` may be:

* an outcome variable when modelling claim severity; or
* a variable being summarised during exploratory analysis.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Variable type}
\neq
\text{Variable role}
}
$$

The role of a variable depends on the question being investigated.

### An Insurance Dataset

Consider the following simplified motor insurance dataset.

Each row represents an insurance policy.

| Policy | Age | Area  | Exposure | Claims | Claim Amount |
| -----: | --: | ----- | -------: | -----: | -----------: |
|      1 |  24 | Urban |     1.00 |      1 |       12,500 |
|      2 |  42 | Rural |     1.00 |      0 |            0 |
|      3 |  31 | Urban |     0.50 |      2 |        8,400 |
|      4 |  56 | Rural |     1.00 |      0 |            0 |
|      5 |  27 | Urban |     0.75 |      1 |       21,300 |
|      6 |  45 | Urban |     1.00 |      0 |            0 |

### Reading the Dataset

Different variables describe different aspects of the insurance risk.

* `Age` describes a characteristic of the policyholder.
* `Area` describes the geographical category.
* `Exposure` describes the amount of risk observed.
* `Claims` records the number of observed claims.
* `Claim Amount` records the aggregate claim amount.

The same dataset can therefore be used to investigate several different questions.

### Questions from the Dataset

**Descriptive question**

> How does claim experience vary across different areas?

**Frequency question**

> What is the observed claim frequency?

**Severity question**

> What is the average claim amount among policies with claims?

**Comparative question**

> Does claim experience appear to differ between younger and older policyholders?

Different questions may require different summaries and analytical methods.

### Frequency and Severity

Two fundamental quantities in insurance analysis are **claim frequency** and **claim severity**.

Claim frequency measures the number of claims relative to exposure:

$$
\text{Claim frequency}
=\frac{\text{Number of claims}}
{\text{Exposure}}.
$$

Average claim severity measures the average claim amount among claims:

$$
\text{Average severity}
=\frac{\text{Total claim amount}}
{\text{Number of claims}},
$$

provided that the denominator is positive.

### Frequency x Severity

The two quantities can be combined to obtain a simple measure of expected loss per unit exposure:

$$
\text{Expected loss per unit exposure}
\approx
\text{Claim frequency}
\times
\text{Average severity}.
$$

This provides a simple bridge between insurance concepts and data science.

The quantities are estimated from observed data.

More advanced methods can then investigate how frequency and severity vary with risk characteristics.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

Insurance data contain different types of information about a risk.

**Frequency** describes how often claims occur, while **severity** describes the size of claims.

Both are needed to understand insurance losses.

:::

## Part IV — The Data Science Life Cycle

### The Data Science Life Cycle

A data science project transforms a practical problem into an evidence-based decision.

Although individual projects differ, most involve several common stages:

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \text{Define} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Acquire} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Prepare} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Explore} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Model} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Communicate} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Deploy and Monitor}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

![Data Science Life Cycle](figures/Data_Science_Life_Cycle.png){#fig-lifecycle-slides fig-align="center" width=60%}

### The Life Cycle Is Not Strictly Linear

The stages provide a framework for organising a data science project.

They should not be viewed as a strictly linear sequence.

For example:

* exploration may reveal data-quality problems;
* data preparation may require returning to the data source;
* modelling may reveal that the original question needs reconsideration; and
* monitoring may show that a deployed model needs to be updated.

$$
\boxed{\text{Data science is a cycle, not a one-time process.}}
$$

### 1. Define the Problem

A data science project should begin with a **question or decision**.

It should not begin simply because a dataset or a modelling technique is available.

For an insurance problem, we should establish:

* what decision needs to be supported;
* what outcome is of interest;
* which population or portfolio is being studied;
* what information may be relevant; and
* how the results will be used.

### Example: Defining an Insurance Problem

Suppose an insurer observes differences in motor insurance claim experience.

A useful question is:

> **Which characteristics are associated with differences in claim frequency?**

This is more informative than:

> "We want to analyse the claims data."

The first question identifies the outcome of interest and gives direction to the analysis.

### From Question to Measurable Quantities

A practical question must be translated into quantities that can be measured using data.

For claim frequency, we need information about:

* the number of claims; and
* the corresponding exposure.

Thus,

$$
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Measurable outcome}
\rightarrow
\text{Required data}.
$$

::: {.callout-important}

## Start with the decision, not the model

The choice of statistical or machine-learning method should follow from the problem.

A sophisticated model is not useful if it does not answer a relevant question or support a meaningful decision.

:::

### 2. Acquire the Data

Once the problem has been defined, the next stage is to obtain the required data.

Insurance data may come from:

* policy administration systems;
* claims systems;
* financial records;
* customer databases; and
* external sources.

Data from different systems may need to be combined using a common identifier.

### What Data Are Required?

The required data depend on the question.

For example, analysing claim frequency may require:

* number of claims;
* exposure;
* policy characteristics; and
* relevant risk characteristics.

Data acquisition may involve:

* importing files;
* querying databases;
* accessing APIs; or
* obtaining data from external sources.

### Available Data vs Appropriate Data

Having a large dataset does not guarantee a useful analysis.

We must distinguish between:

$$
\boxed{\text{Available data}}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{\text{Appropriate data}}.
$$

Data are appropriate when they measure quantities relevant to the problem and are suitable for the intended analysis.

### 3. Prepare the Data

Raw data are rarely ready for analysis.

**Data preparation** involves:

* checking;
* cleaning;
* transforming; and
* organising the data.

Common problems include:

* missing values;
* invalid or impossible values;
* inconsistent data types;
* duplicated observations;
* inconsistent categories;
* incorrect dates; and
* observations outside the relevant period.

### Data Preparation in Insurance

Insurance data provide many examples.

For example:

* a policy may have a missing inception date;
* an exposure period may be incorrectly recorded;
* a claim may be linked to an inactive policy; or
* the same geographical area may appear under different labels.

These problems can affect the results of subsequent analysis.

### Data Transformation

Data preparation may also require transformations.

For example:

* converting dates into a standard format; standardising category labels; or
* aggregating several claim records to obtain total claim amount by policy.

The objective is not simply to make the dataset look tidy.

Each transformation should have a clear reason based on:

* the meaning of the data; and the requirements of the analysis.

::: {.callout-note}

## Data cleaning is part of the analysis

Decisions about missing, invalid, or unusual observations can affect the results.

Data preparation should therefore be documented and carried out with an understanding of the underlying insurance process.

:::

### 4. Explore the Data

After the data have been prepared, the next stage is **exploratory data analysis (EDA)**.

The purpose of EDA is to understand the main characteristics of the data before formal modelling.

EDA can examine:

* distributions of variables;
* differences between groups;
* relationships between variables;
* unusual or extreme observations;
* missing values; and
* possible data-quality problems.

### Numerical and Graphical Exploration

EDA uses both numerical summaries and graphical methods.

**Numerical summaries** include:

* mean;
* median;
* standard deviation; and
* other descriptive statistics.

**Graphical methods** include:

* histograms;
* boxplots;
* bar charts; and
* scatterplots.

Different methods reveal different features of the data.

### EDA in Insurance

Suppose an insurer wants to understand differences in claim experience.

EDA might be used to:

* compare claim frequency across geographical areas;
* examine the distribution of claim amounts;
* identify unusually large claims; and
* investigate relationships between age and claim experience.

EDA can reveal patterns that require further investigation.

### EDA Before Modelling

Exploration is more than a preliminary presentation of the data.

It may reveal:

* variables that require transformation;
* groups that should be examined separately;
* unusual observations; or
* relationships that require further investigation.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Explore}
\rightarrow
\text{Understand}
\rightarrow
\text{Model}
}
$$

The analysis should be guided by what the data can reasonably support.

### 5. Model the Data

When modelling is required, an appropriate statistical or computational model can be developed.

A model provides a mathematical representation of relationships in the data.

Depending on the problem, the objective may be to:

* explain observed patterns;
* estimate an unknown quantity; or
* predict future outcomes.

### Insurance Modelling Examples

Data science models can be used for:

* claim frequency;
* claim severity;
* probability of a claim;
* future claims; and
* expected losses.

The appropriate model depends on:

* the nature of the outcome;
* the available data;
* the purpose of the analysis; and
* the assumptions that can reasonably be made.

### Different Outcomes Require Different Models

The number of claims is a **count variable**.

Claim amount is a **monetary variable**.

These outcomes have different characteristics and may therefore require different modelling approaches.

The model should follow from the problem and the nature of the data.

### Model Evaluation

Model development should include evaluation.

A model that fits historical data well may not necessarily provide reliable predictions for new observations.

Therefore, we need to assess whether the model is:

* appropriate for the problem;
* consistent with its assumptions; and
* useful for its intended purpose.

::: {.callout-important}

## A model is an approximation

A statistical model does not reproduce reality exactly.

It provides a simplified representation of relationships observed in the data.

Its usefulness depends on whether its assumptions and results are appropriate for the problem being considered.

:::

### 6. Communicate the Results

The results of an analysis must be communicated clearly to the people who will use them.

A technically correct analysis has limited value if its findings cannot be understood or connected to the original decision.

Communication may involve:

* tables;
* charts and visualisations;
* written reports;
* presentations; or
* interactive dashboards.

### Communicate for the Audience

The form of communication should reflect the audience.

For example:

**Actuarial report**

* assumptions;
* methodology;
* model performance; and
* technical interpretation.

**Senior management**

* main findings;
* important limitations; and
* implications for the decision.

The same analysis may therefore require different forms of communication.

### From Results to Decisions

Good communication should connect the results back to the original question.

For example, instead of simply reporting:

> Group A has a higher observed claim frequency than Group B.

the analysis should explain:

* the size of the difference;
* the evidence supporting it;
* relevant limitations; and
* possible implications for the insurance decision.

A useful structure is:

$$
\text{Problem}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Interpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{Implication}.
$$

### 7. Deploy and Monitor

When a model is intended for operational use, the final stage is to **deploy and monitor** it.

**Deployment** means making the model available within the process for which it was developed.

For example, a predictive model might be incorporated into an underwriting system to estimate risk when a new policy is quoted.

### Before Deployment

Deployment should normally be preceded by appropriate testing.

The model should be checked in an environment that reflects its intended use before it is introduced into production.

The objective is to ensure that the model behaves as expected when used in practice.

### Why Monitoring Is Necessary

A deployed model should not simply be left unchanged.

Over time, the following may change:

* insurance portfolios;
* customer behaviour;
* economic conditions;
* claim patterns; and
* data-generation processes.

A model that performed well when developed may therefore become less appropriate later.

### What Should Be Monitored?

Monitoring may include:

* predictive performance;
* data quality;
* unusual changes in input variables; and
* differences between predicted and observed outcomes.

For example, suppose a claim prediction model consistently underestimates claim frequency for a particular segment.

The model may need to be:

* investigated;
* recalibrated; or
* redeveloped.

### The Complete Life Cycle

The complete process is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Define}
\rightarrow
\text{Acquire}
\rightarrow
\text{Prepare}
\rightarrow
\text{Explore}
\rightarrow
\text{Model}
\rightarrow
\text{Communicate}
\rightarrow
\text{Deploy and Monitor}
}
$$

However, the process does not end with deployment.

Monitoring can lead back to earlier stages.

### The Life Cycle Is Iterative {.small}

For example:

$$
\text{Monitor}
\rightarrow
\text{New problem}
\rightarrow
\text{New data}
\rightarrow
\text{New analysis}.
$$

Similarly:

$$
\text{Explore}
\rightarrow
\text{Data-quality problem}
\rightarrow
\text{Prepare again}.
$$

$$
\text{Model}
\rightarrow
\text{Poor performance}
\rightarrow
\text{Reconsider the model or data}.
$$

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

**Data science is a cycle, not a one-time process.**

The objective is to develop solutions that remain useful as the data, environment, and decision-making requirements change.

:::

### From an Insurance Question to a Decision

The life cycle can be viewed as a continuous process:


$$
\boxed{
\text{Insurance Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Data}
\rightarrow
\text{Analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Actuarial Judgement}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision}
\circlearrowleft
}
$$

Each stage contributes to turning an insurance problem into an evidence-based decision.



## Part V — Roles in a Data Science Team

### Roles in a Data Science Team

Data science projects often involve people with different areas of expertise.

The responsibilities may overlap, especially in smaller organisations, but different roles typically contribute different skills.

Common roles include:

- **Data analyst** — understands and communicates information in data.
- **Data scientist** — develops analytical and predictive models.
- **Data engineer** — builds and maintains data infrastructure.
- **Actuary** — applies risk and insurance expertise to the problem.

### Data Science Team Roles

![Core Roles and Responsibilities in a Data Science Team](figures/Data_Science_Team_Roles.png){#fig-team-roles-slides fig-align="center" width=85%}

The exact responsibilities depend on the organisation.

In a small organisation, one person may perform several roles.

In a larger organisation, responsibilities may be distributed among specialists.

### Data Analyst

A **data analyst** focuses on understanding and communicating information contained in data.

Typical activities include:

- preparing data for analysis;
- producing descriptive statistics;
- identifying patterns and trends;
- creating tables and visualisations; and
- communicating findings to stakeholders.

For example, an insurance data analyst might examine claim frequency by geographical area and report differences in observed experience.

The role is closely associated with the **exploration and communication** stages of the data science life cycle.

### Data Scientist

A **data scientist** typically works on more complex analytical and predictive problems.

The role may involve:

- statistical modelling;
- predictive modelling;
- machine learning;
- model evaluation; and
- translating analytical results into useful information for decision-making.

For example, a data scientist might develop a model to predict the probability that a motor insurance policy will generate a claim.

The distinction between a data analyst and a data scientist is not always strict.

### Data Engineer

A **data engineer** focuses on the infrastructure and processes required to make data available for analysis.

Typical activities include:

- collecting data from different systems;
- building and maintaining data pipelines;
- storing and organising data;
- integrating data from multiple sources; and
- ensuring that data can be accessed reliably.

For example, an insurer may have separate systems for policies, claims, and payments.

A data engineer may develop processes that extract and combine these data for analysis.

### The Actuary in a Data Science Team

For an actuarial student, an important question is:

> **Where does the actuary fit within a data science team?**

Actuaries contribute specialised knowledge of:

- risk and uncertainty;
- insurance products;
- financial consequences;
- actuarial methods; and
- the decisions that analytical results are intended to support.

### Actuarial Contribution to a Data Science Project

For example, when developing a motor insurance pricing model, an actuary may contribute by:

- defining the insurance problem;
- identifying appropriate measures of exposure;
- selecting relevant risk characteristics;
- assessing whether modelling assumptions are reasonable;
- interpreting model results in an insurance context; and
- considering implications for pricing and risk management.

### Comparing the Roles

| Role | Main focus | Example in insurance |
|---|---|---|
| Data analyst | Describe and communicate data | Analyse claim experience |
| Data scientist | Develop analytical and predictive models | Predict claim frequency |
| Data engineer | Build and manage data infrastructure | Combine policy and claims data |
| Actuary | Apply risk and insurance expertise | Interpret results for pricing |

The boundaries between these roles are not fixed.

An actuary may perform data analysis and statistical modelling, while a data scientist may need substantial knowledge of the insurance problem.

### Skills Across the Life Cycle

Different roles contribute to different stages of the data science life cycle.

$$
\begin{array}{c}
\text{Acquire and prepare data}
\\
\downarrow
\\
\text{Explore and analyse}
\\
\downarrow
\\
\text{Model}
\\
\downarrow
\\
\text{Interpret and communicate}
\\
\downarrow
\\
\text{Decision}
\end{array}
$$

No single role necessarily owns the entire process.

### Data Science Is Collaborative

A successful data science project usually requires more than one type of expertise.

Technical skills are needed to:

- work with data;
- build analytical systems; and develop models.

Domain knowledge is needed to:

- formulate the right problem;
- understand the meaning of the data; and
- interpret the results appropriately.

::: {.callout-note}

## For actuarial students

Developing data-science skills does **not** mean replacing actuarial methods with machine learning.

Data science provides additional tools for applying actuarial knowledge to increasingly complex data and decision-making problems.

:::

## Part VI — Applications of Data Science in Insurance

### Data Science in Insurance

Data science can be applied throughout the insurance value chain.

Insurers collect data at many stages, from:

- underwriting and policy administration;
- claims settlement;
- customer interactions; and
- portfolio management.

These data can support decisions about risk, operations, and business performance.

### Applications Across the Insurance Value Chain

![Data Science Applications in the Insurance Industry](figures/Data_Science_in_Insurance_Applications.png){#fig-insurance-apps-slides fig-align="center" width=78%}

The methods may differ across applications, but the underlying data-science principles remain similar.

### Common Applications

Major applications include:

1. **Pricing and underwriting**
2. **Claims management**
3. **Fraud detection**
4. **Customer analytics**
5. **Risk management and forecasting**

Each application begins with an insurance problem and uses relevant data to support a decision.

### Pricing and Underwriting

Pricing is one of the main applications of data science in insurance.

Insurers need to estimate the expected cost of claims and determine premiums that appropriately reflect the risks being insured.

Historical policy and claims data can be used to investigate how outcomes vary with:

- age;
- geographical area;
- vehicle characteristics;
- coverage; and
- other risk factors.

### Example: Motor Insurance Pricing

Suppose an insurer wants to investigate whether claim frequency varies with policyholder age.

Historical data can be used to:

1. measure claim experience;
2. explore differences between age groups;
3. identify relevant risk characteristics; and
4. develop a statistical model.

The model can then estimate expected claim frequency for different combinations of risk characteristics.

### Frequency and Severity in Pricing

A simple representation of expected loss is

$$
\text{Expected loss}
\approx
\text{Expected frequency}
\times
\text{Expected severity}.
$$

Data science can support both components.

Historical data can be used to model:

- the number of claims; and
- the amount of individual claims.

Other variables can then be used to explain differences in risk.

### Data Science Does Not Replace Actuarial Pricing

A predictive model provides estimates based on data and modelling assumptions.

A pricing decision may also require consideration of:

- expenses;
- capital;
- reinsurance;
- regulatory requirements;
- market conditions; and
- professional judgement.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

**A predictive model is one input into an actuarial pricing decision.**

It does not determine the final premium by itself.

:::

### Claims Management

Claims generate a substantial amount of information that can be analysed.

Data science can support:

- understanding claim patterns;
- estimating expected claim costs;
- predicting claims outcomes; and
- claims triage.

For example, claims may be classified according to:

- type;
- estimated cost;
- complexity; or
- likelihood of requiring further investigation.

### Using Data to Prioritise Claims

Predictive models can help identify claims that are likely to:

- become large; or
- require additional attention.

This can help claims staff allocate resources more effectively.

The objective is not necessarily to automate the entire claims process.

Analytical results can instead provide additional information to claims professionals when making decisions.

### Monitoring Claims Experience

Data can also be used to monitor the development of claims over time.

For example, observed claim experience can be compared with:

- previous experience; or
- expected outcomes.

Differences may provide information for claims management and portfolio monitoring.

### Fraud Detection

Insurance fraud can result in financial losses and affect the overall cost of insurance.

Data science can help identify claims or transactions with unusual characteristics.

Relevant information may include:

- policy characteristics;
- claim characteristics;
- claim timing;
- claim amounts; and
- previous claims.

### Identifying Unusual Claims

Statistical or machine-learning methods can identify patterns associated with claims that require further investigation.

The model may identify a claim as unusual.

However:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Unusual pattern}
\neq
\text{Proof of fraud}
}
$$

### Prediction Is Not Proof

A model can:

- identify unusual patterns;
- estimate probabilities; or
- rank cases according to predicted risk.

It does **not** automatically establish that a particular policyholder has committed fraud.

::: {.callout-important}

## Prediction is not proof

A data-science model can identify patterns or assign a probability to an outcome.

The result should not automatically be interpreted as proof that fraud has occurred.

Further investigation and appropriate professional procedures are required.

:::

### Customer Analytics

Data science can also be used to understand customer behaviour and interactions with insurers.

Examples include analysing:

- policy renewals;
- cancellations and lapses;
- customer enquiries;
- product preferences; and
- interactions with digital services.

### Example: Policy Lapse

Suppose an insurer wants to identify policies with a high probability of not being renewed.

Historical policy data can be used to:

1. identify previous renewal patterns;
2. develop a predictive model;
3. identify characteristics associated with higher lapse rates; and
4. support decisions about customer communication.

The results may inform:

- customer communication;
- product design; and
- service delivery.

### Risk Management and Forecasting

Data science can support broader risk-management and forecasting activities.

Insurers need to monitor changes in their portfolios and anticipate future outcomes.

Historical data can be used to identify:

- trends;
- changes in risk characteristics; and
- unusual patterns.

### Examples of Forecasting Applications

Examples include:

- forecasting claim volumes;
- monitoring changes in claim severity;
- analysing portfolio composition;
- identifying emerging patterns of loss; and
- supporting scenario analysis.

Forecasting methods use historical patterns and other relevant information to estimate future outcomes.

### Forecasts Are Uncertain

A forecast is subject to uncertainty.

Future insurance experience may differ from historical experience because of changes in:

- economic conditions;
- technology;
- regulation;
- customer behaviour; or
- the underlying risk environment.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Historical pattern}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Certain future outcome}
}
$$

Forecasting requires both statistical analysis and careful interpretation.

### From Data to Insurance Decisions

The applications above use different methods, but they share a common process:

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \text{Insurance problem} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Relevant data} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Analysis or model} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Evidence} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Actuarial judgement} -->
<!-- \rightarrow -->
<!-- \text{Decision}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

$$
\boxed{
\text{Problem}
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{Data}
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{Model}
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{Evidence}
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{Judgement}
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{Decision}
}
$$

This is the same data-science life cycle introduced earlier.

## Part VII — Putting the Ideas Together

### Data Science Across Insurance

Data science is not a single insurance technique.

It is a collection of methods that can support different types of insurance decisions.

The same general process applies to:

- pricing;
- claims management;
- fraud detection;
- customer analytics; and
- risk management.

### One Framework, Many Applications

| Application | Main question | Example output |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing | How does expected loss vary with risk? | Risk estimate |
| Claims | Which claims require attention? | Claim classification |
| Fraud | Which cases are unusual? | Investigation priority |
| Customer analytics | Which policies may lapse? | Lapse probability |
| Risk management | What may happen in the future? | Forecast |

The analytical methods differ, but the underlying process is similar.

### The Common Process

$$
\boxed{
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Data}
\rightarrow
\text{Analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision}
}
$$

The process connects technical data analysis with the original insurance problem.

### Data Science and Actuarial Judgement

Data science provides methods for extracting information from data.

Actuarial knowledge provides the context needed to:

- formulate the insurance problem;
- understand the data;
- assess assumptions;
- interpret results; and
- consider the consequences of a decision.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Data science}
+
\text{Actuarial knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{Better-informed insurance decisions}
}
$$

### Key Ideas from the Chapter

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- explain why data science is relevant to insurance;
- describe the four foundations of data science;
- identify common sources and types of insurance data;
- describe the data science life cycle;
- explain the roles of different members of a data science team;
- identify major applications of data science in insurance; and
- explain how data-driven evidence is combined with actuarial judgement.

### The Big Picture

The central idea of this chapter is:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{Insurance problem}
\\[4pt]
\downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{Relevant data}
\\[4pt]
\downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{Data science life cycle}
\\[4pt]
\downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{Evidence}
\\[4pt]
\downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{Actuarial judgement}
\\[4pt]
\downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{Insurance decision}
\end{array}
}
$$

Data science provides a framework for turning data into evidence.

Actuarial knowledge provides the context needed to interpret that evidence and use it appropriately.

### Looking Ahead

The next chapters will develop the tools needed to work through this process.

We will move from the general framework introduced here to practical methods for:

- working with data;
- exploring and visualising data;
- applying statistical methods; and
- using computational tools for data analysis.

The objective is to connect these methods to actuarial and insurance problems.
